content_voiceover: Mantle cell lymphoma typically presents in patients around fifty eight to sixty three years old, and unlike marginal zone lymphoma it behaves aggressively despite sometimes looking deceptively indolent clinically. Over eighty percent of patients present with stage three or four disease, and extranodal involvement is the rule rather than the exception, occurring in about ninety percent of cases, including bone marrow, peripheral blood, liver, and notably the GI tract, where it classically causes multiple lymphomatous polyposis. Bone marrow involvement is found in fifty three to ninety percent of patients, and a full quarter of patients present with a leukemic phase. Among those with leukemic involvement, seventy four percent have concomitant splenomegaly, thirty nine percent show blastoid transformation, which is a more aggressive morphologic variant, and six percent have central nervous system involvement, an important consideration for prognosis and treatment planning. On immunophenotype, the tumor cells express CD19, CD20, and CD22, plus CD5, but critically they are CD23 negative, which is the key feature distinguishing mantle cell lymphoma from CLL slash SLL on flow cytometry. They're also CD10 negative. The molecular hallmark is the translocation t eleven fourteen involving IGH and CCND1, which drives cyclin D1 overexpression, confirmed by immunohistochemistry as seen in the brown staining on this slide.
keypoints: Aggressive B cell lymphoma, median age 58 to 63, stage III/IV in over 80%
90% extranodal involvement, including GI tract lymphomatous polyposis
CD5 positive but CD23 negative distinguishes it from CLL/SLL
Hallmark t(11;14)(q13;q32) drives cyclin D1 overexpression
Blastoid variant and CNS involvement signal higher risk disease
keypoint_voiceover: Key exam points here: mantle cell lymphoma is CD5 positive but CD23 negative, unlike CLL, it carries the t eleven fourteen translocation causing cyclin D1 overexpression, and watch for blastoid morphology or CNS involvement as markers of more aggressive disease.
